title: Node.js TSC vote on the future of primordials

events.summary: A TSC member opens a vote issue on primordials, listing possible goals (tamper-proof everything, only module loading, selectively by performance) and approaches (primordials, C++, other), and asks for input on which modules belong in the subset before voting in two weeks.
A TSC member asks what implement means in the options.
The opener suggests migrate is the better word.
A TSC member reframes the options as subset-only migration, migrate everything handling performance cliffs case by case, and an ill-defined status quo.
The opener rewords, distinguishing continued migration with trade-offs from freezing until a new approach appears.
The member asks whether freezing is really the status quo, which he understood as using primordials except in hot paths.
The opener says migration had stopped after performance drops and rewords that option as leaving migration where it is.
A TSC member recommends a multiple-choice vote like the earlier Promises vote.
The opener agrees but wonders how to run it on GitHub.
A TSC member suggests ranked-choice voting via OpaVote as used for the Corepack vote.
The opener asks two members which modules should, should not, or may be migrated.
A TSC member wants all modules migrated and says the subset referred to the loader.

A TSC member asks for very specific voting options with pros and cons, and proposes a numbered list ranging from loader-only primordials or C++ to undoing all primordials or surveying the community, plus benefit criteria.
The opener worries that many options will confuse voters, since the brainstorm aimed to prune poor choices.
The opener restructures the options into goals and approaches after a TSC meeting.
The member says checking goals would need multi-step voting, and argues primordials rarely deliver robustness because user code itself breaks under tampering.
Another member replies that users control their apps but not Node, so an unfixable core problem differs from a fixable app one.
The opener posts the ten options presented at the 8 December TSC meeting and asks which to exclude.

A TSC member proposes agreeing on test cases rather than a dependency list, and splitting the vote into how tamper-proof core should be and how to achieve it, noting different areas of core deserve different answers.
A TSC member suggests ranked choice since tamper-proofing is not binary.
A TSC member reports meeting consensus to drop three options and the REPL ones, leaving five choices.
He argues to remove the community-survey option as a further delay and the freeze option as the worst of all worlds, and asks whether the bind-this option means waiting for V8.

A TSC member raises an unlisted alternative: isolate tamper-proof code in a separate loader thread behind minimal IPC, notes CJS cannot realistically be tamper-proof, and warns C++ hurts contributor accessibility.
A TSC member links a real user report where tampering with array prototypes broke console.log, as evidence of the robustness users expect.
A TSC member explains the bind-this option would use proposal syntax with a build step to transpile it, not wait for V8.
The member links Deno's decision to adopt primordials.
A TSC member notes the bind-this proposal is on the TC39 agenda, later deferred to January.
A TSC member supports dropping the community-survey option, expecting it would only delay.
A TSC member asks the 20 members who intends to abstain, to plan how to decide.
A TSC member will vote asynchronously.
A TSC member will abstain, seeing merit on both sides.
A TSC member adds the issue to the TSC meeting agenda.
A TSC member asks whether bind-this is about making primordials ergonomic enough.
A TSC member confirms and adds it may become standard idiom.
A TSC member reports from the meeting that upcoming ESM changes will make ESM and policy tamper-proof anyway, so the vote should focus on other modules such as repl, http and console.
A TSC member asks for reading on how that would work.
The member links the meeting recording where it was explained.

A TSC member proposes six refined vote options, from fully tamper-proof via moving off the main thread through primordials-if-no-perf-regression to no primordials at all, and suggests separate votes per area, starting with the error path.
A TSC member asks what the options apply to and what porting away from JS means, and now plans to vote.
A TSC member summarises the ESM answer as moving loaders off-thread.
The proposer says the scope will be defined per vote and clarifies the off-thread option, which he does not favour.
A comment GitHub marks as hidden (duplicate).
A TSC member accidentally closes the issue.
She reopens it immediately.
She apologises for pressing the wrong button.
She leans toward moving the REPL and loader off JS or the main thread, doubts primordials guarantee tamper-proofing, and says JS loader code is not easier to read in practice.
A TSC member formally calls a first vote limited to code on the error path, with six options, and invites objections to scope or wording.
A TSC member notes bind-this would not remove the need for some primordials and helpers, though more readable.
A TSC member cites the charter rule that a vote call needs a majority to second it, seconds it, and asks members to thumbs-up his comment.
A TSC member thumbs it up but plans to abstain for lack of context.
A TSC member supports a vote.
He pings the TSC to weigh in on moving to a vote.
A TSC member asks to define the error path before voting.
The proposer defines it as code that runs before or inside an unavoidable throw, excluding shared public APIs.
A TSC member asks who will set up the voting mechanism.
The opener asks the proposer to run the vote.
A TSC member asks for the error-path definition.
The proposer links the definition and offers to run the vote if votes are public, since he is involved.
The member asks what full tamper-proofing would require, what stream changes it implies, and why only the error path.
A TSC member questions the value, since tamper-proofing the error path matters less than the normal path.
The proposer says it is a starting point where reliability likely beats performance, and explains the result would govern which PRs can land or be blocked.
A TSC member says he mainly cares about the non-error path.
A TSC member supports the vote but asks what the options apply to.
A TSC member counts 11 seconds, a majority, and declares the vote on.
A TSC member opens a PR to hold the error-path vote with a new tool for encrypted ballots committed to a branch, counted by the Condorcet method after about two weeks.
The proposer links the voting PR #1158.
A TSC member asks where the tool's source is, since a file seems missing.
The organiser says the stray file is gone and the repo and package are in sync.
The member thanks him.
A comment GitHub marks as hidden (off-topic).
A TSC member likes the tool.
A comment GitHub marks as hidden (off-topic).
A TSC member asks whether higher scores mean stronger preference.
The organiser confirms any integer scale works, highest for most preferred.
The member thanks him.
A TSC member asks how to vote.
The proposer points to the voting PR.
The organiser reminds the TSC to vote before it closes.
The organiser explains how to abstain while marking a disliked option.
A TSC member hits a permissions bug in the shell voting script and reports it.
He reports the web ballot omitted author info and adds it by hand.
A TSC member renames his ballot file to his handle.
The organiser explains how the handle is chosen for file names.
The member notes he used a command without the handle flag.
The organiser fixes the tool to sanitise file names.
A TSC member likes the voting method.
A TSC member likes it too but objects that the encryption relies on one person holding the key.
The organiser agrees trust should be distributed, perhaps via key splitting or CI, in a future version.
A TSC member argues topic votes should be public like legislative votes and encryption could be dropped.
A TSC member thinks a trustless design is possible and that the key will be revealed after the vote.
The organiser keeps encryption so voters cannot influence each other, but agrees ballots should end up public.
The organiser suggests moving the trust discussion to its own thread.
The member agrees and says he has a rough design.
The organiser announces the vote closes by end of day.

The organiser posts results: with about 86% participation, the winning option allows error-path primordials provided performance does not regress significantly, ahead of dropping prototype-method primordials.
A TSC member is confused whether the winning option endorses or limits primordials.
A TSC member reads it as accepting primordials in error paths unless they regress performance.
The organiser adds that removing error-path primordials would be refused unless they cause measurable regressions, and agrees future wording should be clearer.
A TSC member asks whether that means writing error-path benchmarks.
A TSC member asks whether the PR should now land.
The organiser says ballots must be decrypted first and a participation record added.
A TSC member thinks benchmarks would be required, so a pending error-path PR would be blocked.
A TSC member asks about code outside the error path.
A TSC member says that was out of scope and more votes should follow.
A TSC member thought error-path performance was not a concern at all, and only effects on normal paths would block a change.
A TSC member agrees error-path performance has never been a priority.
The organiser suggests a formatting fix to the results file.
The organiser marks the vote PR ready for review.
A TSC member approves.
The member says voting on the error path before the main path made him vote conservatively.
The opener of the issue says his vote is missing from the results file.
The organiser adds the missing ballot, which ranked moving off the main thread highest.
The organiser apologises for the omission and links the fix.
The issue opener approves.
A TSC member approves.
A TSC member questions why the performance option was offered if it is treated like full tamper-proofing, suggesting the vote might have gone differently.
A TSC member reports the meeting agreed to close this issue and open new ones for follow-on votes.
The issue is closed.
A TSC member approves after testing the tooling.
The vote PR is merged.
The vote PR closes on merge.
The organiser links a Node core PR adding primordials guidelines to the docs.
A contributor later links a docs PR about using primordials when coding.
